hook_text: Two South African tragedies of the First World War. Why was one remembered for decades, and the other almost forgotten?
clip_script: July 1916. Delville Wood, France. About 3 150 white South African soldiers are ordered to hold a wood at all costs. Six days of shelling. About 780 answer the roll call. A grand memorial follows in 1926. February 1917. Fog off the Isle of Wight. The troopship Mendi, carrying black South African labourers, is rammed and sinks in twenty minutes. 616 South Africans die. Their families get no medals, no national memorial. Only after 1994 does South Africa honour them too.
visual_style: A whiteboard split between a shattered wood on the Somme and a ship sinking in fog, then two memorials appearing decades apart.
pacing: Builds the two stories in parallel, then contrasts their memory.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson to master Delville Wood and the Mendi.
